lessons.title: Azure Subscriptions and Management Groups

slots.practicalActivity: In your own Azure subscription, run az account show and az account list --output table to see every subscription your account can reach, then create a resource group named rg-az104-lab in your nearest region — you'll keep using this same resource group across this course's Azure chapters. If your account has management-group creation rights, run az account management-group create to create one test management group and move rg-az104-lab's subscription under it with az account management-group subscription add; if it doesn't, read the Portal's Management Groups blade instead and write one sentence identifying your tenant's Tenant Root Group.
slots.deliverable: Real az account show/list output identifying your active subscription, a created rg-az104-lab resource group you'll reuse all course, and either a real management group with your subscription added or a written identification of your tenant's Tenant Root Group.

lessons.title: Resource Groups and Azure Resource Manager

slots.practicalActivity: Create a second, scratch resource group with az group create --name rg-arm-scratch, deploy a single storage account into it from a minimal ARM template JSON (matching the lesson's example) using az deployment group create, then run the exact same deployment a second time and confirm in the output that ARM reports no changes — proving idempotence for yourself. Finally, apply a CanNotDelete lock to rg-az104-lab with az lock create and confirm az group delete against it actually fails while the lock is active.
slots.deliverable: A storage account deployed twice from the same ARM template with the second run's no-change output captured, plus a CanNotDelete lock on rg-az104-lab confirmed by a failed delete attempt.

lessons.title: Azure Regions and Resource Naming Conventions

slots.practicalActivity: Run az account list-locations --output table and identify your nearest region plus its real paired region from Microsoft's documented pairings. Using the resource-type-prefix / workload / environment / region / instance naming convention from the lesson, write out the full name you'd give rg-az104-lab if you were naming it fresh today, and apply that intended name as a Name tag on it (resource groups can't actually be renamed once created).
slots.deliverable: Your nearest region and its real paired region from az account list-locations, plus a convention-compliant name written out for rg-az104-lab and applied to it as a tag.

lessons.title: Tags, Azure Policy, and Cost Governance Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Apply Environment=Training, CostCenter=1000, and an Owner tag to rg-az104-lab with az group update --tags, then in the Portal's Azure Policy blade assign the built-in 'Require a tag on resources' policy scoped to rg-az104-lab and confirm it shows as assigned. Finally, create a real monthly budget (a few dollars is enough) for rg-az104-lab with az consumption budget create, including an 80% alert threshold pointed at your own email.
slots.deliverable: rg-az104-lab tagged with Environment/CostCenter/Owner, a built-in tag-requiring Azure Policy assigned and confirmed scoped to it, and a real small monthly budget with an 80% email alert threshold created on it.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra ID: What It Actually Is

slots.practicalActivity: In the Azure Portal, open Microsoft Entra ID and record your tenant's name, tenant ID, and primary onmicrosoft.com domain from its Overview page. Sign out of portal.azure.com and sign back in, paying attention to the redirect, and write two sentences explaining — using what you now know about Graph API calls over HTTPS instead of LDAP/Kerberos — what's actually happening during that redirect that wouldn't happen with on-prem Active Directory.
slots.deliverable: Your real tenant name, tenant ID, and onmicrosoft.com domain recorded from Entra ID's Overview page, plus two written sentences explaining the Graph-API-based sign-in flow versus on-prem AD.

lessons.title: Users, Groups, and Licenses in Entra ID

slots.practicalActivity: In Microsoft Entra ID, create one new cloud-only test user and set their department attribute to Finance. Create a security group named sg-finance with dynamic membership rule department -eq "Finance" and confirm your test user is added automatically within a few minutes. If your tenant has a spare license (a free trial license works), assign it to sg-finance via group-based licensing and confirm the user inherits it; if not, open the group's Licenses blade and write one sentence describing what assigning a license there would do.
slots.deliverable: A real cloud-only test user with a Finance department attribute, a dynamic security group (sg-finance) that added them automatically, and either a confirmed group-based license inheritance or a written explanation of what one would do there.

lessons.title: Azure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

slots.practicalActivity: On rg-az104-lab, open Access control (IAM) and assign your test user (or a second real account) the Reader role scoped specifically to that resource group — not the subscription. Confirm in the Role assignments tab that the Scope column actually reads the resource group. Then write out the exact role-assignment equation (security principal + role definition + scope) for this assignment, plus one sentence on what that user still cannot do with Reader that Contributor would allow.
slots.deliverable: A real Reader role assignment on rg-az104-lab confirmed scoped to the resource group (not the subscription) in IAM's Role assignments tab, plus the written principal+role+scope equation and the Reader-vs-Contributor limitation.

lessons.title: Conditional Access and MFA Basics

slots.practicalActivity: If your tenant has Entra ID P1 (or a trial), create a Named Location under Security > Named locations for your home/office IP, then build a real Conditional Access policy targeting sg-finance that requires MFA whenever the sign-in location is NOT that named location. If your tenant has no P1 license, instead open Entra ID's Security defaults blade, record whether it's enabled, and write out the if-this-then-that condition/control breakdown for that same Finance policy as if you were configuring it.
slots.deliverable: Either a real Conditional Access policy created and scoped to sg-finance with a documented named-location condition and MFA control, or your tenant's Security defaults status plus a written condition/control breakdown of the Finance MFA example.

lessons.title: Creating and Sizing an Azure Virtual Machine

slots.practicalActivity: Inside rg-az104-lab, run a real az vm create for an Ubuntu VM sized Standard_B1s (burstable, cheap to leave running briefly) with --admin-username and --generate-ssh-keys, then SSH into it once it's up to confirm it's actually reachable. Run az vm image list --output table, find one image with no short alias, and write down its full publisher:offer:sku:version URN.
slots.deliverable: A real, running Ubuntu VM in rg-az104-lab confirmed by a successful SSH login, plus one full Marketplace image URN found via az vm image list for an image with no short alias.

lessons.title: VM Availability Sets and Availability Zones

slots.practicalActivity: In rg-az104-lab, create an Availability Set with az vm availability-set create and deploy one small VM into it using --availability-set. Separately, deploy a third VM pinned to a specific zone with --zone. Run az vm list --output table to compare all three VMs' placement, then write one sentence explaining which of the three would survive an entire datacenter outage and which would not.
slots.deliverable: Three real VMs in rg-az104-lab — one in an Availability Set, one zone-pinned, one with neither — with az vm list output and a written sentence identifying which placement actually survives a full datacenter outage.

lessons.title: Managed Disks and VM Storage Options

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real data disk with az disk create at the Premium_LRS tier, attach it to one of your lab VMs with az vm disk attach, then SSH in and confirm the OS sees a second disk with lsblk. Create a second disk at Standard_LRS for comparison, and write two sentences matching each tier to the right workload from the lesson (a transactional database vs. a backup archive).
slots.deliverable: A Premium_LRS data disk attached to a lab VM and confirmed visible with lsblk, plus a second Standard_LRS disk created for comparison and two written sentences matching each tier to the right workload.

lessons.title: Virtual Machine Scale Sets Basics

slots.practicalActivity: In rg-az104-lab, create a real Virtual Machine Scale Set with az vmss create at an initial instance count of 2, then attach an autoscale rule with az monitor autoscale create and az monitor autoscale rule create that scales out when average CPU exceeds 70% for 10 minutes. Confirm the scale set and its instances with az vmss list-instances --output table, then delete the scale set once confirmed, since it's the most expensive resource you've created this chapter.
slots.deliverable: A real VMSS with 2 instances and a working autoscale-out rule confirmed via az vmss list-instances, torn down afterward once verified.

lessons.title: Storage Accounts and Performance Tiers

slots.practicalActivity: In rg-az104-lab, create a real storage account with a globally unique name using az storage account create at the Standard tier and StorageV2 kind, then run az storage account show to confirm its kind and SKU. Create a second storage account at the Premium tier and compare the two az storage account show outputs side by side, noting exactly which fields differ.
slots.deliverable: Two real storage accounts (Standard and Premium tier) created in rg-az104-lab, with az storage account show output for both captured and the differing fields noted.

lessons.title: Blob Storage: Containers and Access Tiers

slots.practicalActivity: In your Standard storage account, create a container named db-backups with az storage container create, then upload 3 small test files at three different tiers — one Hot, one Cool, one Archive — using az storage blob upload --tier. Attempt to download the Archive-tier blob directly and confirm it fails or requires a rehydration request first, then compare that against the Hot and Cool blobs, which download immediately.
slots.deliverable: A real db-backups container with one blob each at Hot, Cool, and Archive tier, plus confirmation that the Archive blob required rehydration while the Hot and Cool blobs downloaded immediately.

lessons.title: Azure Files and Azure Disks Compared to Blob

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real Azure file share with az storage share create, then mount it from your lab VM over SMB (use the Portal's 'Connect' blade to get the exact mount command for your OS) and write one file to it. Separately, confirm your Lesson 11 managed disk is still attached to exactly one VM with az disk show --query managedBy, and write a 3-row comparison table (Blob, Azure Files, Managed Disk) naming which of your own real resources fills each row.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure file share mounted and written to from your lab VM, confirmation a managed disk is attached to exactly one VM, and a completed Blob/Azure Files/Managed Disk comparison table using your own real resources.

lessons.title: Storage Redundancy (LRS/ZRS/GRS) and Lifecycle Management

slots.practicalActivity: Change one of your storage accounts' redundancy to GRS with az storage account update --sku Standard_GRS, then run az storage account show --query secondaryLocation to confirm Azure assigned it a real paired-region secondary. Create a real lifecycle management policy on that account (matching the lesson's JSON) that tiers db-backups blobs to Cool after 7 days, Archive after 90, and deletes them after 365, using az storage account management-policy create.
slots.deliverable: A storage account updated to GRS with its real secondary region confirmed, plus a real lifecycle management policy applied to db-backups enforcing the 7/90/365-day Cool/Archive/delete schedule.

lessons.title: Virtual Networks and Subnets in Azure

slots.practicalActivity: In rg-az104-lab, create a real VNet with az network vnet create using address prefix 10.30.0.0/16 and a first subnet 10.30.1.0/24, then add two more subnets (10.30.2.0/24 and 10.30.3.0/24) with az network vnet subnet create. Run az network vnet subnet list --output table and, for your smallest subnet, calculate and write down exactly how many usable addresses remain after Azure's 5 reserved addresses.
slots.deliverable: A real VNet in rg-az104-lab with 3 non-overlapping subnets confirmed via az network vnet subnet list, plus a written usable-address calculation for the smallest one after Azure's 5 reservations.

lessons.title: Network Security Groups in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real NSG with az network nsg create, add an Allow-HTTPS rule at priority 100 for port 443 from the Internet service tag and an Allow-SSH-Admin rule at priority 110 scoped to only your own public IP, then attach the NSG to one of your VNet's subnets with az network vnet subnet update. Try reaching port 22 from a different network (a phone hotspot or different Wi-Fi) and confirm it's blocked, then try from your admin IP and confirm it works.
slots.deliverable: A real NSG attached to a subnet with an Allow-HTTPS rule open to the internet and an Allow-SSH rule scoped to one IP, with SSH confirmed to fail from an unlisted network and succeed from the admin IP.

lessons.title: Public IPs and Azure Load Balancer Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Create a Standard SKU public IP with az network public-ip create, then create a Standard Load Balancer in front of two lab VMs from earlier chapters with az network lb create, az network lb probe create (TCP port 80), and az network lb rule create. Confirm the backend pool's health, then deliberately stop one VM and re-check the pool to see it marked unhealthy and pulled from rotation.
slots.deliverable: A real Standard Load Balancer with a health probe and rule in front of 2 lab VMs, confirmed healthy, then re-checked after stopping one VM to show it marked unhealthy and removed from rotation.

lessons.title: VNet Peering and Connecting Azure Networks

slots.practicalActivity: Create a second small VNet (10.40.0.0/16) in rg-az104-lab, then peer it to your Lesson 17 VNet with two az network vnet peering create calls — one from each side — and confirm both report Connected. Deploy one small test VM into the new VNet and SSH to a VM in the original VNet across the peering to confirm private connectivity actually works, then write one sentence on why this would NOT let a third, unpeered VNet reach either of these two.
slots.deliverable: Two real peered VNets with both peering links confirmed Connected, cross-VNet connectivity verified with a real SSH session, and a written sentence on peering's non-transitivity.

lessons.title: Getting Started with the Azure CLI

slots.practicalActivity: Run az account list --output table against your real account to see every subscription you can reach, then az account set --subscription to explicitly target the one holding rg-az104-lab. Run the same az vm list query three ways — --output table, --output json, and --output tsv — and compare the outputs side by side. Finally, run a --query JMESPath filter that reshapes the output to just each VM's name, size, and resource group.
slots.deliverable: Real az account list/set output confirming your active subscription, az vm list captured in all three output formats, and one working --query JMESPath filter reshaping VM output to name/size/resource group.

lessons.title: Managing Resources with az Commands

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's full 4-step lifecycle for real against a fresh scratch resource group: az group create, az vm create inside it, az resource list to see every resource type the VM create actually produced (disk, NIC, public IP, VNet), and finally az group delete --yes --no-wait to tear it all down in one call. Count exactly how many resource types az resource list returned and write them down.
slots.deliverable: A real create-inspect-delete lifecycle run against a fresh scratch resource group, with az resource list output listing every resource type the single az vm create call actually produced.

lessons.title: Azure PowerShell Cmdlets for Administrators

slots.practicalActivity: Install the Az PowerShell module with Install-Module -Name Az -Scope CurrentUser, run Connect-AzAccount and Get-AzSubscription, then Set-AzContext to the subscription holding rg-az104-lab. Run Get-AzVM -ResourceGroupName rg-az104-lab to list your real lab VMs, then create and delete one throwaway resource group with New-AzResourceGroup and Remove-AzResourceGroup -Force, comparing each PowerShell command against its CLI equivalent from Lesson 22.
slots.deliverable: A working Az PowerShell session confirmed with Get-AzSubscription/Set-AzContext, real Get-AzVM output for rg-az104-lab, and a resource group created and removed with New-AzResourceGroup/Remove-AzResourceGroup.

lessons.title: Azure Cloud Shell and Scripting Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Open Azure Cloud Shell (shell.azure.com or the Portal icon), confirm it mounts a persistent Azure Files share as $HOME, and save a small script there. Write and run the lesson's Bash for loop (or the PowerShell foreach version) that lists every resource group your account can see and every resource inside each one, using --query and --output tsv. Close the session, reopen Cloud Shell a few minutes later, and confirm your saved script is still there.
slots.deliverable: A real Cloud Shell session with a working for/foreach loop listing every resource group and its resources via --output tsv, plus confirmation the saved script persisted across closing and reopening the session.

lessons.title: Azure Monitor and Metrics Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Open one of your lab VMs' Overview page and chart its real Percentage CPU metric in Metrics Explorer, switching the aggregation from Average to Maximum over the last 24 hours and noting whether the chart's shape changes. Then pull the identical metric from the command line with az monitor metrics list --resource <vm-resource-id> --metric "Percentage CPU" --interval PT1H and confirm the CLI output matches what the portal chart showed.
slots.deliverable: A real Percentage CPU metrics chart for a lab VM shown at both Average and Maximum aggregation, plus matching az monitor metrics list CLI output for the same metric.

lessons.title: Log Analytics and the Activity Log

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real Log Analytics workspace with az monitor log-analytics workspace create, then open your subscription's Activity Log and filter it by your own account to find the real entries for several resources you've created and deleted so far this course. Run a KQL query against AzureActivity filtered to the last 24 hours and summarized by OperationNameValue, matching the lesson's example exactly.
slots.deliverable: A real Log Analytics workspace created, your own filtered Activity Log entries confirmed for several of this course's earlier actions, and one working KQL query against AzureActivity summarized by operation.

lessons.title: Alerts and Action Groups

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real Action Group with az monitor action-group create that emails you, then create a metric alert on a lab VM with az monitor metrics alert create at condition "avg Percentage CPU > 80" over a 5-minute window, pointed at that Action Group. Deliberately generate real CPU load on the VM (e.g. a few background yes > /dev/null loops, or a short stress-ng run) and confirm the alert actually fires and you receive the email.
slots.deliverable: A real Action Group and CPU metric alert created on a lab VM, with the alert confirmed to have actually fired (and the email received) after deliberately generating CPU load.

lessons.title: Cost Management and Budgets

slots.practicalActivity: Open Cost Management + Billing and run Cost analysis grouped by resource group, then grouped by tag, confirming your Lesson 4 tags actually show up as a grouping option. Create a real budget scoped to rg-az104-lab for a small dollar amount with two alert thresholds (80% and 100%) using az consumption budget create, matching the lesson's exact JSON notification structure.
slots.deliverable: Real Cost analysis views grouped by both resource group and tag, plus a real budget on rg-az104-lab with 80%/100% alert thresholds created via az consumption budget create.

lessons.title: Lab: Deploying a Small Multi-Tier Environment
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Deploying and Administering an Azure Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's full Briarcliff Systems deployment for real, command by command: az group create for briarcliff-rg with environment/costcenter/owner tags, a VNet split into web-subnet and app-subnet, a web-tier VM with a public IP in web-subnet, an app-tier VM with --public-ip-address "" in app-subnet, and a Standard_LRS storage account for application data. Confirm with az resource list that all 5 pieces exist and that app-vm1 genuinely has no public IP by checking its NIC.
slots.deliverable: A real 5-resource multi-tier environment (tagged resource group, 2-subnet VNet, public web VM, no-public-IP app VM, storage account) deployed exactly as the lesson specifies, confirmed with az resource list and a NIC check proving app-vm1 has no public IP.

lessons.title: Lab: Securing and Monitoring the Environment
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Deploying and Administering an Azure Environment

slots.practicalActivity: On the briarcliff-rg environment from Lesson 29, run the lesson's exact commands: create web-nsg allowing 80/443 from Internet and app-nsg allowing only port 8080 from the web subnet's CIDR (with an explicit Deny-Internet-Inbound at priority 200), attach both NSGs to their subnets, assign a test group Virtual Machine Contributor scoped only to the resource group, create an action group plus a high-CPU metric alert on the web VM, and set a $150 monthly budget with an 80% alert threshold.
slots.deliverable: Real NSGs enforcing the web/app tier boundary, an RBAC role assignment scoped to the resource group (not the subscription), a working CPU metric alert with its action group, and a $150 budget with an 80% threshold — all confirmed against the lesson's exact commands.

lessons.title: Case Study: Troubleshooting a Cost Spike
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Deploying and Administering an Azure Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Deliberately recreate the lesson's incident in a real scratch resource group: deploy an oversized VM (Standard_D4s_v3 or similar) with a Premium_LRS disk and leave it running, then practice the diagnosis exactly as the lesson does — az costmanagement query grouped by ResourceId to find the expensive resource, az vm show to confirm its size and running state, and az disk list to check its disk tier. Apply the real fix: az vm deallocate, az vm resize down to Standard_B2s, and az disk update to StandardSSD_LRS.
slots.deliverable: A deliberately oversized VM+disk diagnosed using az costmanagement query/az vm show/az disk list exactly as the lesson walks through, then actually fixed with deallocate, resize, and a disk-tier downgrade.

lessons.title: Chapter Capstone: Azure Administration Review
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Deploying and Administering an Azure Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Walk your entire rg-az104-lab and briarcliff-rg environments end to end and write a one-paragraph architecture summary covering: which governance decisions (tags, naming) were made before any compute existed, how RBAC was scoped at each point, which VM sizes and storage tiers you chose and why, how the subnet/NSG boundary enforced tier separation, and which monitoring/cost alerts are still live. Then delete every resource group you created this course with az group delete --yes --no-wait and confirm with az group list that your subscription is clean again.
slots.deliverable: A written end-to-end architecture summary covering governance, RBAC scope, compute/storage sizing, the networking tier boundary, and live monitoring/cost alerts, followed by confirmation via az group list that every lab resource group was deleted and the subscription is clean.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can administer a real Azure environment end to end: governing it with resource groups, tags, and Azure Policy; managing identity and access through Entra ID users, groups, and precisely scoped RBAC role assignments; provisioning and sizing virtual machines, managed disks, and VM Scale Sets for the right workload; choosing the right storage account, blob access tier, and redundancy option for real cost/durability tradeoffs; building VNets, subnets, NSGs, load balancers, and peered networks that actually enforce a multi-tier security boundary; working equally comfortably in the Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, and Cloud Shell; and watching what they've built with Azure Monitor metrics, Log Analytics/KQL, alerts, and Cost Management budgets — then has personally diagnosed and fixed a real cost-spike incident and torn down everything they deployed.
